A natural contrarian though I may be, I have to be a genuine hater here, I did not enjoy Snatch . I'm not intimately acquainted with the genre - or the culture these films aim to 'replicate' - but this feels like parody, and not in a particularly entertaining way. While there is some semblance of stylism in the editing, the majority of these instances range from boring to tacky. The burning caravan scene is cool, and I like the POV shots of characters lying on the ground with others literally looming over them, but it’s too overused to be effective. They try to mix it up with Dutch angles to the same end, but it doesn't work for me. Powerpoint transitions, GTA split screens and rotating jpegs, I know we're living it up in the year 2000, but this looks so cheap in modern viewing. The colours are washed out to emulate a sort of grittiness but the grimmer moments just fall flat for me in the direction. The music is weirdly jaunty at moments where it doesn't quite gel with what's happening (put a pin in that) and Errol & Tony are the only marginally intimidating performances, everyone else feels a bland. Much like a lot of the dialogue, a lot of these performances feel like they’re read directly off the page. Oh man the dialogue draaaaaags. Every time Sol, Vincent and Tyrone are on screen I'm begging for them to just get on with it, every conversation feels like: The car crashes, "you just crashed the car," "why did you do that?" "yeah, why did you do that?" "well, I didn't do it on purpose," "yeah, you shouldn't have done that," "yeah" ...Like, if this is parody, I'm sure it's brilliant, but fuck me, maybe I'm too brain-rotted by instagram reels and better action films, I'm so bored, I do not care. There are some moments that tap into the inherent poetry of the cockney dialect, my favourite being 'as bent as the Soviet sickle, and as hard as the hammer that crosses it' but the majority borders on cringe. The pacing is so slow, yet whenever something interesting happens, it's over before it's even started. Anticlimactic first boxing match, anticlimactic bookie heist, anticlimactic gun shots to the head, I have no idea what we're working towards here. It feels like the same scene over and over again in pursuit of a 86-carat Macguffin. Jason Statham narrates intermittently but it's unclear why he is the POV character for the majority of this film. When the diamond conveniently happens to him at the very end, there is slight satisfaction of things coming together, but it doesn't feel particularly clever or meaningful. I wouldn't mind if there was some other sort of interesting spectacle happening at any point, but there's nothing here. The final boxing match is slightly better than any of the action pieces before it, but it's not a scratch on the Sherlock Holmes (2009) boxing match, also directed by Guy Ritchie, which is disappointing. An... interesting role for Brad Pitt...everyone saying Pitt is incomprehensible is crazy, I easily understand it, or maybe I'm just someone who is northern and actually interacts with people outside of my dialect. It always bothers me when they get A-Listers to play poor people with their perfect Hollywood teeth, though of course Pitt's performance isn't the only elephant-sized/shaped issue with the framing of the traveller community in this film. Take a shot for every racial slur - if you thought The Gentleman was bad, Snatch will give you a stroke. The Jewish stereotyping is also pretty egregious. Musically, there's this grotesquely hokey Yiddish scoring whenever a Jewish person in on screen, though arguably it specifically appears only when 'fake Jews' are on screen, i.e., The Head and the costumed thieves in the opening. If we're being charitable, this sonic stereotyping could be an exercise in satirical hyperrealism to draw attention to the false semitic surface, but I think it's unlikely. From what I understand in his other work that I've heard, John Murphy ranges from competent but boring in James Gunn's Superman (2025), to the brilliance of 28 days later , so this could swing either way. Messy, directionless, dull, and confusing in tone - this one just wasn't for me.

as far as action movies go, this one was about as close to a 12 year old boys fever dream as you can get. It’s two whole hours of complete chaos and i was so confused and lost practically the entire time. It’s like the director said “let’s mash as many tropes as we can into one movie”. You’ve got crime, boxing, killing, gunfights, murder, blackmailing, robberies, heists, and so much more in one single movie and everyone speaks with a heavy indecipherable accent. I figured that was supposed to be funny but because I had no idea which character was which or what was going on, I found it rather irritating. I even paused the movie several times to google the plot summary to decipher what the hell was going on. i mean, why was jason statham’s character the only one who had a narrated inner monologue? Hay algo casi entrañable en la cantidad de directores que salieron de los noventa convencidos de que Quentin Tarantino había descubierto las Américas. Robert Rodríguez entendió la lección como una invitación a convertir la serie bé en una fiesta de sangre, guitarras y sicarios sudorosos disparándose a dos metros de distancia. Danny Boyle recogió la velocidad, la música pop y la insolencia formal, pero tuvo la decencia de añadir desesperación, mugre y cierta idea del mundo en el panorama brit. Guy Ritchie, en cambio, pareció quedarse con la parte más fácilmente vendible del asunto: criminales con gracia, montaje nervioso, canciones muy bien escogidas y la convicción absoluta de que todo mejora si un anglo con gabardina camina a cámara lenta. Y qué mediocre puede llegar a ser Guy Ritchie. Un mediocre con labia, eso sí, que es una categoría particularmente irritante. Porque uno quisiera despreciarlo tranquilamente y, de repente, te hace 'Snatch.'. La película parece anunciar desde el primer minuto: «¿No viste 'Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels'? No importa, aquí está otra vez, pero ahora tenemos dinero y Brad Pitt». Es uno de los reciclajes más descarados del cine contemporáneo y, quizá por eso mismo, uno de los más honestos. Ritchie no pretende haber aprendido nada entre una película y otra. Simplemente ha comprado juguetes mejores. Tenemos diamantes, apuestas ilegales, boxeo clandestino, ladrones ineptos, gánsteres con nombres ridículos, rusos que se niegan a morir y suficientes planes cruzados y tramas que se abren como para mantener ocupados a veinte guionistas que en realidad sólo están contando el mismo chiste: todos estos hombres creen ser profesionales y casi todos son unos completos gilipollas. Ese es el gran hallazgo de esto. No el montaje, no la música, no los movimientos de cámara que Ritchie exhibe como un niño enseñando las funciones nuevas de su videocámara. La verdadera gracia está en que este supuesto universo de hombres peligrosos está compuesto por gente que apenas sería capaz de organizar una barbacoa sin acabar enterrando a alguien. Ritchie, por supuesto, hace todo lo posible para que uno no repare demasiado en ello. Está demasiado ocupado dirigiendo. Nadie puede abrir una puerta normalmente en una película de Guy Ritchie. Nadie puede simplemente conducir un coche. Nadie puede recibir un puñetazo sin que intervengan una cámara lenta, tres ángulos, un ruido seco, una aceleración temporal y alguna canción escogida para recordarnos que lo que acabamos de ver es tremendamente cool . Ritchie es el Don Siegel de los garrulos o el Tarantino de los que no tienen el graduado escolar. Su mayor miedo como cineasta parece ser que una escena permanezca quieta el tiempo suficiente como para que el espectador pueda pensar. Hay planos que prácticamente llevan escrita encima la frase: «¿Has visto qué plano?». Y, sin embargo, funciona. Ahí está lo que jode. Porque 'Snatch' tiene ritmo. Tiene timing y tiene una habilidad extraordinaria para presentar veinte personajes, hacerlos chocar entre sí y conseguir que el espectador siga entendiendo quién quiere matar a quién y por qué. Ritchie convierte el caos narrativo en mecanismo de relojería, aunque el reloj esté cubierto de cerveza, sangre y saliva. Brad Pitt aparece haciendo de gitano y se dedica a destruir el idioma inglés durante el resto de la película. Es probablemente la mejor decisión interpretativa de toda la función. Pitt comprende que en semejante circo no tiene ningún sentido intentar parecer serio, así que construye un personaje basado en tres elementos: músculos, golpes y una dicción que parece proceder de una civilización todavía no catalogada por los lingüistas. Benicio del Toro tiene la sensatez de entrar, parecer importante y desaparecer antes de que Ritchie pueda ponerle demasiados efectos alrededor. Vinnie Jones interpreta algo bastante parecido a la idea que uno tiene de Vinnie Jones después de verlo entrar enfadado en un pub o de la idea que daba como futbolista. Y Alan Ford consigue que su personaje parezca genuinamente desagradable, cosa meritoria en una película donde la mayoría de los criminales parecen haber sido diseñados por una agencia de publicidad especializada en cerveza. Todo tiene una capa de estilización tan espesa que casi puede rascarse con una moneda. Nadie parece vivir realmente en ese Londres: posan dentro de él. Un Londres andrajoso (qué redundante) donde los coches, los bares, los abrigos, las pistolas: todo está colocado con la misma preocupación estética que tendría una campaña de ropa para hombres que fantasean con tener contactos en los bajos fondos. Pero debajo de esa pose hay una comedia que se me hace bola. Cada personaje intenta proyectar autoridad mientras el universo se dedica sistemáticamente a humillarlo: los planes fracasan, los cadáveres reaparecen, los perros se comen cosas que no deben, los boxeadores hacen lo contrario de lo pactado, los tipos duros reciben golpes absurdos. Toda la película consiste básicamente en contemplar cómo el ego masculino es triturado por la incompetencia. El problema es que Ritchie confunde acumulación con complejidad. Sus películas apestan enormemente a inglés, a pub y a fish 'n chips. Hay tantos personajes, desvíos y pequeñas intra-historias que la película parece más elaborada de lo que realmente es, hasta parece una novela de Pynchon de gangsters. Debajo de todo ese montaje frenético hay una trama bastante simple que empieza a agotarse mucho antes del final. Y ahí aparece la paradoja: 'Snatch' no deja de moverse y, aun así, por momentos aburre. La cámara corre, los personajes hablan deprisa, la música entra a golpes, alguien recibe un puñetazo y aparece otro tipo con un apodo gracioso. Pero velocidad no es ritmo, y cortar una escena veinte veces no la vuelve veinte veces más interesante. No diría que sea completamente insoportable, tiene momentos divertidos y bastante oficio. Pero también bostezas varias veces. Y cuando una película tan obsesionada con parecer dinámica consigue aburrirte, quizá el problema sea que Ritchie agita mucho la coctelera y nunca se pregunta si había algo interesante dentro.

In my review of "Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels," Guy Ritchie's 1999 film, I wrote: "In a time when movies follow formulas like zombies, it's alive." So what am I to say of "Snatch," Ritchie's new film, which follows the "Lock, Stock" formula so slavishly it could be like a new arrangement of the same song? Once again we descend into a London underworld that has less to do with English criminals than with Dick Tracy. Once again the characters have Runyonesque names (Franky Four Fingers, Bullet Tooth Tony, Boris the Blade, Jack the All-Seeing Eye). Once again the plot is complicated to a degree that seems perverse. Once again titles and narration are used to identify characters and underline developments. There is one addition of considerable wit: In the previous film, some of the accents were impenetrable to non-British audiences, so this time, in the spirit of fair play, Ritchie has added a character played by Brad Pitt, who speaks a gypsy dialect even the other characters in the movie can't understand. Pitt paradoxically has more success communicating in this mode than some of the others do with languages we allegedly understand. He sounds like a combination of Adam Sandler and Professor Backwards. Ritchie is a zany, high-energy director. He isn't interested in crime, he's interested in voltage. As an unfolding event, "Snatch" is fun to watch, even if no reasonable person could hope to understand the plot in one viewing. Ritchie is almost winking at us that the plot doesn't matter, that it's a clothesline for his pyrotechnics (if indeed pyrotechnics can employ clotheslines, but don't get me started). The plot assembles its lowlifes in interlocking stories involving crooked boxing, stolen diamonds and pigs. After Frankie Four Fingers (Benicio Del Toro) steals a diamond in Antwerp, Belgium, and returns to London, a Russian named Boris the Blade (Rade Sherbedgia) and an American gangster named Avi (Dennis Farina) try to separate him from it--not easy, since it is in a case handcuffed to his wrist. Meanwhile (somehow I don't think "meanwhile" quite says it), a boxer named Gorgeous George is knocked flat, and two shady promoters find themselves in hock to a crime czar. Desperate to find a winner, they recruit the gypsy played by Pitt, who is a formidable bare-knuckle fighter that London gamblers won't recognize. Also, bodies are fed to pigs. Pitt's character and the gypsy community where he lives are the most intriguing parts of the movie. If this summary seems truncated, it's because an accurate description of this movie dialogue might read like the missing chapters from Finnegans Wake . Because the actors have cartoon faces, the action is often outrageous and Ritchie has an aggressive camera style, the movie is not boring, but it doesn't build and it doesn't arrive anywhere. It's hard to care much about any of the characters because from moment to moment what happens to them seems controlled by chance. I mentioned the Marx Brothers in my review of "Lock, Stock" and I thought of them again here, as strangely dressed weirdos occupy an anarchic nightmare. I don't want Ritchie to "grow." I don't care if he returns to the kind of material that worked for him the first time around. I just want him to get organized, to find the through line, to figure out why we would want to see the movie for more than its technique. I can't recommend "Snatch," but I must report that no movie can be all bad that contains the following dialogue: U.S. Customs official: "Anything to declare?" Avi (Dennis Farina): "Yeah. Don't go to England." Note: I am not so crass as to mention in my review that Guy Ritchie and Madonna recently became man and wife. I save such biographical details for my footnotes, and would overlook them altogether, except that it is blindingly clear to me that he should direct, and she should star in, a British remake of "Guys and Dolls."

Scavenger Hunt #138 Film 4 of 30 Category: Watch a film with an ensemble cast The Film *Snatch* is the kind of crime film that seems completely out of control while secretly knowing exactly where every character and storyline is going. What begins with a stolen diamond quickly expands into illegal boxing, fixed fights, gambling debts, violent gangsters, incompetent criminals, and a dog that somehow becomes essential to the entire plot. There are so many characters moving toward different goals that the story could have easily become confusing. Instead, the chaos becomes the main source of entertainment. Everyone thinks they understand the situation, yet almost nobody has any real control over it. Every plan creates another problem, every criminal underestimates somebody, and the diamond keeps moving through the film as though it is mocking everyone chasing it. The comedy works because the characters take their ridiculous world completely seriously. People are threatened, kidnapped, robbed, and killed, but the movie finds humor in their terrible planning, strange personalities, and inability to communicate. It never pauses to announce a joke. The humor comes from watching confidence collapse into panic. The Direction Guy Ritchie directs *Snatch* with an incredible amount of style and energy. The rapid editing, freeze frames, exaggerated sound effects, slow motion, and sudden changes in speed make the film feel like it is constantly moving. Even scenes built entirely around conversation have momentum because of how quickly the dialogue and reactions bounce between characters. The nonlinear structure also makes the film more satisfying. Sequences that initially appear random eventually connect, and small details return with much greater importance. Ritchie repeatedly shows the same event from different perspectives, allowing one character’s victory to become another character’s disaster. The final stretch is especially strong because every storyline begins colliding at once without losing the film’s rhythm. The style occasionally comes close to overwhelming the story, but it fits this particular world. Everything is loud, grimy, fast, and slightly exaggerated. London feels like an enormous criminal maze where everyone knows somebody dangerous, but nobody knows enough to stay out of trouble. The Ensemble The ensemble is the heart of the film. Jason Statham gives Turkish the exhausted energy of someone who knows every situation is getting worse but has no choice except to keep moving. Stephen Graham is hilarious as Tommy, whose nervous reactions make him the perfect partner for Turkish. Brad Pitt nearly steals the entire movie as Mickey. His accent is almost impossible to understand, yet that becomes part of the character’s power. Everyone treats Mickey like an unintelligent outsider because they cannot understand him, but he is constantly more aware than the people attempting to manipulate him. Pitt makes him funny, unpredictable, and genuinely dangerous without ever changing the character’s relaxed attitude. Alan Ford is terrifying as Brick Top because he never needs to become overly emotional. His calmness makes every threat feel more believable. Dennis Farina brings a completely different energy as Cousin Avi, reacting to England and its criminals with constant irritation. Vinnie Jones is also perfectly cast as Bullet Tooth Tony, whose reputation alone is enough to control most rooms. What makes the ensemble especially effective is that no character feels disconnected from the film’s personality. Even people with limited screen time leave an impression. Each performance adds another form of stupidity, confidence, fear, or violence to the story. Conclusion *Snatch* is a ridiculously entertaining mixture of crime, comedy, and controlled chaos. Its story is complicated, but the film never feels weighed down by explanation. It trusts the audience to keep up and rewards that attention by bringing every strange character and seemingly unrelated detail together. The ensemble cast is what makes the entire machine work. No single character has to carry the movie because everyone contributes something memorable to it. Brad Pitt may be the standout, but the real pleasure comes from watching all these personalities collide and ruin one another’s plans. It is stylish without becoming empty, violent without losing its humor, and complicated without becoming impossible to follow. *Snatch* turns criminal incompetence into an art form and somehow makes complete disorder feel perfectly organized.

Ensuite le choix des musiques est magistrale et je pèse mes mots. Plusieurs bangers sont dans ce film et a chaque fois marqué par un moment bien particulier et inoubliable de ce film. Pour finir les thèmes abordés dans ce film sont les gangs et les combats de rues. Choses que j'apprécie voir dans un film. Mais l'originalité de Snatch c'est la comédie.
